props.title: Beyond Tomorrow

sections.content: Beyond Tomorrow represents a fascinating early exploration of the supernatural drama genre, blending elements of romance and holiday sentiment with metaphysical themes. The film's innovative narrative follows three wealthy businessmen who, after dying in a plane crash, remain as ghosts to watch over a young couple they had previously brought together. This setup preceded similar supernatural romance plots in films like Ghost (1990) and The Ghost and Mrs. Muir (1947), establishing an early template for stories where spirits intervene in earthly affairs.

sections.content: The film's director A. Edward Sutherland, known for comedy work with W.C. Fields, brings unexpected warmth to this supernatural tale. The special effects, while modest by today's standards, were innovative for 1940, particularly in scenes depicting the transparent ghosts observing the living. The film shares thematic DNA with It's a Wonderful Life (1946) and A Matter of Life and Death (1946), exploring the intersection between the earthly and spiritual realms while examining human nature and redemption.

Beyond Tomorrow's cast includes Harry Carey, C. Aubrey Smith, and Charles Winninger as the three wealthy benefactors, whose performances ground the supernatural elements in genuine humanity. The film's exploration of life after death influenced later works like Heaven Can Wait (1978) and Defending Your Life (1991), which similarly examine the relationship between the deceased and the living world they've left behind. SUBHEAD: Impact on Holiday Fantasy Films

Though released in 1940, Beyond Tomorrow helped establish conventions for holiday-themed supernatural films, combining elements of Christmas spirit with ghostly intervention. This influence can be traced through works like The Bishop's Wife (1947) and A Christmas Carol (1951), where supernatural beings intervene in human affairs during the holiday season. The film's gentle approach to death and the afterlife offered audiences comfort during the uncertain times of World War II, much as A Guy Named Joe (1943) would do a few years later.
